titleCandidates: n8n Production Security: Three Verifiable Controls

script:
A running n8n container is only availability evidence. It says nothing about who can reach management surfaces, how administrators authenticate, or whether risky configuration remains. In this build, we will create three independently verifiable controls. First, disable the public REST API and its playground when production automation does not need them. Second, move administrative authentication behind SAML single sign-on where the licensed deployment supports it. Third, run n8n's native security audit and turn the result into deployment evidence. The important word is verify. We will not stop at an environment file. Every change gets an observable positive or negative test, and every claim is tied to current n8n documentation.

Start with a disposable or staging instance that matches production configuration, never with an unreviewed change on the live system. Capture only facts that do not reveal credentials: the container image reference, enabled feature flags, endpoint paths and HTTP status codes. Our baseline probe requests the documented API path and the playground path from the same network zone used by operators. Save the response code and timestamp, not response bodies containing workflow metadata. This establishes the before state. Also record whether any integration genuinely consumes the public API. Disabling a required interface is an outage, not hardening. The decision gate is simple: no verified consumer, proceed; a verified consumer exists, keep the API and reduce exposure through network and credential controls instead.

For an instance that does not need the public REST API, set N8N_PUBLIC_API_DISABLED to true in the deployment configuration. n8n explicitly recommends disabling that API when it is not used. Treat this as immutable infrastructure: change the Compose file, Kubernetes manifest or Railway variable source under version control rather than editing a running container. Produce a configuration diff that shows the variable name but redacts unrelated secrets. Then restart or roll out the service through the normal deployment mechanism. A successful restart only proves that the process accepted its configuration. It does not yet prove the API is unavailable, so keep the baseline probe ready for the post-deployment test.

The API playground is a separate surface. Set N8N_PUBLIC_API_SWAGGERUI_DISABLED to true so an operator does not assume the main API switch also documents every interactive route. Keeping both controls explicit makes reviews easier: one flag addresses API availability, and the other addresses the browser-based playground. After rollout, verify the application health endpoint and the editor path before testing denial. This order distinguishes a secure denial from a dead service. If health fails, roll back immediately. If health succeeds but the old API probe still returns its previous successful response, the deployment did not apply the intended configuration and must not be marked complete.

Now rerun the same probe from the same network location. The acceptance test is not a hard-coded status number for every n8n version; it is that the previously usable public API operation is no longer usable while the application remains healthy. Record the new status, a bounded response fingerprint and the deployment revision. Never print API keys or authorization headers in CI logs. Add a second test for the playground route and a third control test for the editor or health path. Together they prove selective denial: the management interfaces are restricted, but the service still runs. If any test disagrees with the expected matrix, stop the release instead of weakening the assertion to make the pipeline green.

Disabling an interface and centralizing identity solve different problems. The first reduces exposed functionality; SSO controls how approved administrators authenticate. Current n8n documentation supports SAML and OIDC for single sign-on and states that configuration requires an instance owner or administrator. It also limits availability by plan, so verify licensing before designing the rollout. Model the trust boundaries visibly: the identity provider authenticates the person, n8n acts as the service provider, and role or access policy determines what the authenticated person may do. SSO does not replace network isolation, least privilege, secret management or backup access procedures. It gives you a centrally governed authentication path that can be tested and revoked.

For a SAML deployment, enable N8N_SSO_SAML_LOGIN_ENABLED and configure exactly one metadata source. n8n documents N8N_SSO_SAML_METADATA for inline XML and N8N_SSO_SAML_METADATA_URL for a fetched document, and says they are mutually exclusive. The configuration validator should therefore fail if both are present or neither approved source is present. Store inline metadata through the platform's secret mechanism, not in the repository. For a URL, require HTTPS and an approved identity-provider host. Before rollout, validate issuer, audience, callback URL, signing certificate lifetime and clock synchronization. These are deployment checks, not invented n8n guarantees, and they reduce the chance that a syntactically valid SAML setup creates an authentication outage.

Test identity changes with a small matrix. One approved test account must complete SSO and reach only its intended role. One unauthorized account must be denied. An expired or deliberately invalid assertion must fail. Finally, exercise the documented recovery or rollback procedure before removing any existing access path. Capture result identifiers and timestamps, never session cookies or assertions. If the positive test fails, revert the SSO activation. If a negative test succeeds unexpectedly, block the release and inspect identity-provider assignments and n8n role mapping. The goal is not a cinematic login animation; it is evidence that identity decisions cross the IdP-to-n8n boundary exactly as designed.

After the targeted controls pass, run n8n audit. The official documentation says the audit can run through the CLI, public API or n8n node; because this build intentionally disables the public API, the CLI is the cleanest demonstration. Execute n8n audit inside the controlled application context and store the report in protected build artifacts. The report groups risk into credentials, database, file system, nodes and instance findings. Do not describe the command as a complete penetration test. It is a native configuration and usage signal. Classify each finding as accepted risk, remediation work or false positive with an owner and due date, and redact identifiers before sharing screenshots.

Finish by turning the demonstration into a release gate. The pipeline checks configuration exclusivity, deploys to staging, verifies application health, proves API and playground denial, runs the identity test matrix, executes the audit and publishes a redacted evidence bundle. Production promotion requires every mandatory check to pass. Keep rollback automatic for health or access failures, while audit findings follow an explicit severity policy rather than an arbitrary zero-findings promise. This is what makes the workflow reusable: configuration, runtime behavior and evidence agree. The result is not a claim that n8n is secure forever. It is a repeatable control loop that reduces attack surface, centralizes administrator authentication and detects regressions before they become invisible production risk.

metadata.title: Harden n8n: Disable the API, Add SSO, Prove It with an Audit
metadata.description:
Harden a self-hosted n8n deployment with three verifiable controls: disable unused API surfaces, configure SAML SSO safely, and turn the native security audit into release evidence. This is a reproducible engineering walkthrough with negative tests, rollback rules and no real credentials.

Synthetic narration is used. Visuals are original procedural diagrams, terminal simulations and configuration examples created for this video.
